title: Dover Beach
description: Probably written in 1851 on the honeymoon at Dover and published in the New Poems of 1867: the most famous short poem of Victorian doubt, spoken by a lover to his beloved at the window of a house on the strait.
plot_or_argument: The speaker describes the calm sea, the cliffs and the moonlit strait, and hears in the tide the 'eternal note of sadness'; he recalls Sophocles hearing the same note on the Aegean, and the poem turns to the 'Sea of Faith' that was once full and is now retreating, leaving the world a 'darkling plain' of ignorant armies clashing by night.
narrative_structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
meter_and_prosody: Dramatic text. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The author's characteristic manner is classical plainness of diction and a limited, repeated vocabulary.
historical_context: The 1851 honeymoon, the geological and biblical criticism of the 1850s-60s, and the publication of the poem at a moment (1867) when the doubt it articulates had become a public controversy after Essays and Reviews (1860) and the Colenso affair.
literary_significance: 'Dover Beach' is the most quoted Victorian poem and the definitive lyric of the retreat of faith; its 'darkling plain' and 'ignorant armies' have become permanent English images, and the poem's structure of a private love scene carrying a public argument is the model for the modern meditative lyric.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1867, as lyric in irregular unrhymed lines, by Matthew Arnold. Composed between 1851 and 1867. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Culture and Anarchy: An Essay in Political and Social Criticism
description: The founding text of English cultural criticism, first published as a series of essays in the Cornhill Magazine in 1867-68 and collected in 1869: an argument that the state must promote 'culture' — the best that has been thought and said — against the anarchy of class interest and the 'machinery' of Victorian liberalism.
plot_or_argument: The argument proceeds by a survey of English society as three classes — the Barbarians (aristocracy), the Philistines (middle class) and the Populace (working class) — each of which Arnold finds wanting in 'sweetness and light'; the remedy is the cultivation of the 'best self' through education and the action of the state, which Arnold calls 'the organ of our collective best self'.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is classical plainness of diction and a limited, repeated vocabulary.
historical_context: The 1867 Reform Act and the Hyde Park riots, the campaign for national education, the disestablishment of the Irish Church, and the Victorian debate between Nonconformist voluntarism and state action.
literary_significance: Culture and Anarchy gave English criticism its vocabulary and its central problem: the relation of culture to democracy. 'Philistine', 'Barbarian', 'sweetness and light' and 'culture' as Arnold defines it all derive from this book, and its argument shaped the English debate on education and the state from Huxley and Spencer to the Newbolt Report and the founding of English studies.

bibliographical_notes: Published by Smith, Elder in January 1869; the essays had appeared in The Cornhill Magazine from July 1867 to February 1868, with the preface added. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Essays in Criticism
description: The first series of 1865 collects the essays that established Arnold as the leading critic of the age — 'The Function of Criticism at the Present Time', 'The Literary Influence of Academies', 'Maurice de Guérin', 'Eugénie de Guérin', 'Heine', 'Joubert', 'Spinoza and the Bible', 'Marcus Aurelius' — and the second series of 1888 adds the essays on Wordsworth, Byron, Shelley, Gray, Keats and Tolstoy.
plot_or_argument: The central argument, stated in 'The Function of Criticism', is that criticism must be disinterested: it must 'learn and propagate the best that is known and thought in the world' and must resist the practical, party and personal considerations that make English criticism provincial. The essays on French and German writers are examples of that disinterestedness applied to English culture.

The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is classical plainness of diction and a limited, repeated vocabulary.
historical_context: The 1860s: the periodical culture of the Cornhill and the Fortnightly, the Victorian ignorance of continental literature, and the crisis of religious belief that Arnold addressed in the same years. The record dates the work as composed between 1863 and 1888 and first published in 1865 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.

title: Literature and Dogma: An Essay towards a Better Apprehension of the Bible
description: Published in 1873 and the central work of Arnold's later religious criticism: an attempt to save the Bible and the Christian moral tradition from both the dogmatic theologians and the scientific sceptics by treating the biblical language as 'literature' and 'poetry' rather than as metaphysics.
plot_or_argument: Arnold argues that the word 'God' in the Bible is used as a term of 'the Eternal, not ourselves, that makes for righteousness', not as the name of a metaphysical person; the book examines the language of the Bible, the meaning of miracles and prophecy, and the 'Aberglaube' (extra-belief) that has overlaid the original 'verifiable' experience of righteousness.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.

The author's characteristic manner is classical plainness of diction and a limited, repeated vocabulary.
historical_context: Darwin's Origin (1859) and Descent (1871), Essays and Reviews (1860), the Colenso controversy and the new biblical criticism, and the Victorian debate on the disestablishment of the Irish Church (1869).
literary_significance: Literature and Dogma is the classic Victorian attempt to preserve religious experience after the collapse of dogmatic belief, and it invented the modern idea of the Bible as literature; its influence on Pater, on the modernist theology of the twentieth century and on the study of the Bible in English departments has been continuous.

title: On the Study of Celtic Literature
description: Four lectures delivered as Professor of Poetry at Oxford in 1865-66 and published in 1867: the founding English study of Celtic literature, and the text in which Arnold set out his influential and contested theory of the Celtic 'genius'.
plot_or_argument: Arnold surveys the Welsh, Irish and Gaelic literary remains, argues that English literature owes to Celtic a quality of 'natural magic' and sentiment which it needs, and calls for the study of Celtic at Oxford; the argument is conducted with Arnold's characteristic mixture of sympathy and condescension toward the 'Celtic race'.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The text is the printed lecture, retaining the spoken address. The author's characteristic manner is classical plainness of diction and a limited, repeated vocabulary.
historical_context: The 1860s Celtic revival, the Welsh Sunday Closing agitation and the Irish land question, and the new philology of the 1860s. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1867 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.

title: The Wreck of the Deutschland
description: Written in 1875-76 on the wreck of the Deutschland, which sank in the Thames estuary in December 1875 with five Franciscan nuns among the drowned; offered to the Month and refused, and unpublished until the 1918 edition: the first poem in sprung rhythm.
plot_or_argument: The ode opens with the poet's personal address to God, turns to the shipwreck and to the tall nun's cry 'Christ, King, Head', and ends in a prayer for the conversion of England; the wreck is read as an instance of divine mastery and of the 'harvest' of the tall nun's faith.
narrative_structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
meter_and_prosody: Dramatic text. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The metre is sprung rhythm, with the number of stresses fixed and the number of unstressed syllables free. The form is the ode, in irregular or regular stanzas.
historical_context: The Deutschland disaster of 7 December 1875, the Jesuit province of North Wales where Hopkins was studying, the conversion of England for which the Jesuits prayed, and the Oxford Movement's legacy. The record dates the work as composed between 1875 and 1876 and first published in 1918 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
literary_significance: The Wreck of the Deutschland is the greatest English religious ode of the century and the work in which sprung rhythm was invented; its rejection by the Month kept Hopkins's poetry unpublished in his lifetime and its publication in 1918 changed the technique of English verse.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Written in 1875-76 and refused by The Month; it was first printed in the Poems of 1918. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Windhover: To Christ Our Lord
description: Written on 30 May 1877, the day after his ordination, and the most famous of Hopkins's sonnets: the kestrel's flight read as an image of Christ's mastery and of the beauty that 'buckles' the self. It is a verse work of 1918 by Gerard Manley Hopkins; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: The octave watches the kestrel hovering and describes its mastery in compound epithets; the sestet turns from the bird to Christ and to the paradox that the 'sheer plod' of ordinary labour and the 'blue-bleak embers' of a dying fire are more beautiful than the bird's brilliance, because they 'fall, gall themselves, and gash gold-vermilion'.
narrative_structure: A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the fourteen-line sonnet, Petrarchan or Shakespearean, and in sequences where the individual sonnets accumulate into a continuous argument or a narrative of feeling. The metre is sprung rhythm, with the number of stresses fixed and the number of unstressed syllables free. The form is the fourteen-line sonnet.
historical_context: The 1877 ordination, the Welsh landscape of St Beuno's, and the Ignatian meditation on created things as the 'footprints' of God. The record dates the work as composed in 1877 and first published in 1918 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
literary_significance: 'The Windhover' is the most anthologised Victorian sonnet after 'God's Grandeur' and the technical showpiece of sprung rhythm; it is the central English poem of the sacramental imagination, and its critical history (from Bridges's puzzlement to the modern readings of Empson and others) is a case study in the reception of difficulty.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1918, as petrarchan sonnet in sprung rhythm, by Gerard Manley Hopkins. Composed in 1877. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: God's Grandeur
description: Written in 1877: a sonnet on the grandeur of God in the world and the human refusal to see it — 'the world is charged with the grandeur of God' — and one of the founding texts of modern nature poetry.
plot_or_argument: The octave states the presence of God's grandeur in the world and the way 'generations have trod, have trod, have trod' until the ground is seared; the sestet turns to the renewal of the world by the Holy Ghost, whose brooding over the bent world makes it 'warm with the grandeur of God' again.
narrative_structure: A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

Verse in the fourteen-line sonnet, Petrarchan or Shakespearean, and in sequences where the individual sonnets accumulate into a continuous argument or a narrative of feeling. The metre is sprung rhythm, with the number of stresses fixed and the number of unstressed syllables free. The form is the fourteen-line sonnet.
historical_context: The industrial England of the 1870s, the Jesuit training in Lancashire and Wales, and the 1877 sermons on the created world as the manifestation of God. The record dates the work as composed in 1877 and first published in 1918 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.

title: The Terrible Sonnets
description: The 'terrible' or 'sonnets of desolation' written in Dublin in 1885-88 — 'Carrion Comfort', 'No worst, there is none', 'To seem the stranger lies my lot', 'I wake and feel the fell of dark, not day', 'Patience, hard thing!', 'My own heart let me more have pity on' — and the most powerful English poems of spiritual desolation.
plot_or_argument: The sonnets record the loss of consolation in prayer: the soul wrestles with a God who seems to withhold grace, the mind is reduced to 'the mind's own self-taste', and the sequence ends in the effort to accept the will of God without the feeling of his presence.
narrative_structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
meter_and_prosody: Dramatic text. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The metre is sprung rhythm, with the number of stresses fixed and the number of unstressed syllables free. The form is the fourteen-line sonnet.
historical_context: Hopkins's Dublin years as Professor of Greek at the Royal University, his isolation in Ireland, his failing health and his conflict with the political and religious atmosphere of the country, and the spiritual theology of the dark night.
literary_significance: The terrible sonnets are the central documents of Victorian religious suffering and the greatest devotional poems in English of the nineteenth century; their analysis of depression has made them permanent texts of the modern literature of mental illness, and their influence on the twentieth-century religious lyric is direct.

title: Binsey Poplars
description: Written in March 1879 after the felling of the poplar trees along the Isis at Binsey, near Oxford: the most quoted English poem of ecological mourning and one of the clearest statements of Hopkins's doctrine of inscape.
plot_or_argument: The poem records the felling of the aspens 'that dandled a sandalled shadow', laments that the 'sweet especial rural scene' can never be restored, and ends with the warning that 'ten or twelve' strokes of the axe 'unselve' the countryside.
narrative_structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order.
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The metre is sprung rhythm, with the number of stresses fixed and the number of unstressed syllables free.
historical_context: The felling of the Binsey poplars in 1879 and the Victorian destruction of rural landscape by industry and agriculture, which Hopkins addressed in several poems and letters. The record dates the work as composed in 1879 and first published in 1918 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet.

title: Goblin Market and Other Poems
description: Published in 1862 with illustrations by Dante Gabriel Rossetti, and the volume that made her reputation: Goblin Market, 'Remember', 'A Birthday', 'After Death', 'The Convent Threshold', 'Up-Hill' and 'An Apple Gathering'.
plot_or_argument: In Goblin Market, Laura buys and eats the goblins' fruit and begins to waste away, calling for 'more'; her sister Lizzie resists the merchants' assault and returns with the juice of the fruit on her face, which restores Laura; the poem ends with the two as wives and mothers telling the story to their children.
narrative_structure: A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
principal_characters: Laura; Lizzie; the goblin men; Jeanie
literary_form: Poetry collection; title poem in irregular rhymed couplets
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The verse runs in rhymed couplets. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is simple quatrains and ballad stanzas with exact rhyme.
historical_context: The 1860s, the Pre-Raphaelite circle and its treatment of the fallen woman, the Victorian debate on sensual temptation and the spiritual reading of fairy tale, and the penitentiary work at Highgate where Christina Rossetti taught from 1876.
literary_significance: Goblin Market is the most discussed Victorian poem by a woman and a central text of modern feminist criticism, read as an allegory of consumerism, of sexual knowledge, of sisterhood and of the Eucharist; its fairy tale surface and its theological depth made it the model for the fantastic moral tale from MacDonald and Kingsley to the modern fantasy.

bibliographical_notes: Published by Alexander Macmillan in April 1862, with illustrations by Dante Gabriel Rossetti; the volume made the author's reputation and she was proposed for the laureateship in 1896. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Prince's Progress and Other Poems
description: Published in 1866 with illustrations by her brother: the title poem, a ballad-allegory of the prince who delays on his journey and finds the princess dead, together with 'The Convent Threshold', 'A Royal Princess', 'Under the Rose' and the devotional lyrics.
plot_or_argument: The prince sets out to claim his bride, is delayed by the temptations of the road, and arrives to find her dead; 'A Royal Princess' concerns a princess who gives her wealth to the poor; 'Under the Rose' is the monologue of a great lady's illegitimate daughter, brought up in the village and never acknowledged.
narrative_structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
principal_characters: the Prince; the waiting bride; the milkmaid; the alchemist; the Royal Princess; the unacknowledged daughter of 'Under the Rose' and her mother, 'my Lady'
literary_form: Poetry collection; title poem in ballad stanzas
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The stanza is the ballad stanza, the four-stress and three-stress lines rhyming on the even lines. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is simple quatrains and ballad stanzas with exact rhyme.
historical_context: The 1860s Pre-Raphaelite interest in the ballad and the allegory, the Victorian cult of the dead virgin (Elizabeth Siddal died in 1862), and the Anglo-Catholic devotional culture of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1861 and 1866 and first published in 1866 and the corpus places it within Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
literary_significance: The Prince's Progress is the finest Victorian allegorical ballad and the clearest statement of Rossetti's theology of delay and loss; its treatment of the princess's autonomy (as against the prince's dilatoriness) has made it a key text in the modern reading of her gender politics.

title: Sing-Song: A Nursery Rhyme Book
description: Published in 1872 with illustrations by Arthur Hughes: 120 nursery rhymes, riddles, lullabies and poems on natural history written for and about children, and one of the foundation texts of English children's verse.
plot_or_argument: The poems are short lyrics on the moon, the wind, birds, flowers, death and sleep, many of them in question-and-answer form or in dialogue with a child; some are riddles whose answers lie in the natural world.
narrative_structure: A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is simple quatrains and ballad stanzas with exact rhyme.
historical_context: The 1870s and the new market for illustrated children's books (Caldecott, Crane, Greenaway), the Victorian cult of childhood, and the mortality rates among children that the poems accept without evasion.
literary_significance: Sing-Song is one of the purest bodies of children's verse in English and a central document in the history of Victorian children's literature. Its frank treatment of death and its formal perfection have made it a permanent text for the study of the Victorian child, and it influenced de la Mare and the children's poets of the twentieth century.

title: A Pageant and Other Poems
description: Published in 1881, containing 'A Pageant', 'Monna Innominata: A Sonnet of Sonnets', 'The Key-Note' and the devotional and elegiac lyrics of her later manner: the volume in which she turns fully to the preparation for death.
plot_or_argument: 'Monna Innominata' is a sequence of fourteen sonnets in which a woman speaks the unspoken love of the great Tuscan poets, prefaced by an argument that the Lady of the sonnet tradition has never spoken for herself; 'A Pageant' is a series of visionary poems on the months and on mortality.
narrative_structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order.
literary_form: Poetry collection, including the sonnet sequence 'Monna Innominata'
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The form is the fourteen-line sonnet. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is simple quatrains and ballad stanzas with exact rhyme.
historical_context: The 1880s, her increasing illness (Graves' disease diagnosed in 1871), the devotional life at Highgate, and the aesthetic movement's cult of the sonnet. The record dates the work as composed between 1879 and 1881 and first published in 1881 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet.

Its preface to Monna Innominata is a founding text for the feminist criticism of the sonnet tradition, and the volume's death poems are among the greatest English devotional lyrics.

description: Privately printed in 1893 for the Society of the Sacred Cross and reprinted in 1896 as New Poems: the devotional verse and prose of her last years, including 'The World', 'A Better Resurrection' and the poems on the Eucharist.
